food.text: Much of the food of the Dorset people is thought to have come from hunting sea mammals that breathe through holes in the ice. They were highly adapted to living in a very cold climate. Their late phase lasted from 500 to 1000 CE.
The Norse settlements founded in Greenland after 986 CE rested on three pillars: livestock farming, hunting and catching animals. Together these provided food and trade goods in varying proportions.

Norse Greenlanders kept cattle, sheep, goats, dogs and cats on scattered fjord farms. They also hunted seal and caribou, and walrus for trade. Their main hunt was the Nordrsetur, a communal spring hunt of migratory harp seals.
Livestock breeding in Greenland required large pasture areas, so the Norse farms were widely separated from each other. As a result they were effectively self-sufficient.

Ice-core and clam-shell data suggest that between AD 800 and 1300, southern Greenland's fjord regions had a relatively mild climate, several degrees warmer than usual for the North Atlantic. This allowed trees and herbaceous plants to grow, and made livestock farming and barley cultivation possible near the 70th parallel. Yet the Icelandic Book of Settlements also records harsh winters, with famines reportedly leading to the killing of "the old and helpless" who "were killed and thrown over cliffs".

Bad harvests hit Iceland in the 970s. Along with a famine, they helped push people to look for new settlement areas, even though a stable social structure had been established and good land was legally owned. That search led to the Norse settlement of Greenland.

Around the mid-10th century the Medieval Warm Period began to warm the Arctic considerably, and the sea ice became less predictable. This massive decline in sea-ice would have strongly affected the Dorset, whose food depended on hunting at the ice. They could have followed the ice north.

Erik the Red, an outlawed chieftain, established a settlement in Greenland in 985. Its early settlers sailed westward in search of better pasturage and hunting grounds. This was after Gunnbjörn Ulfsson got lost in a storm and sighted the Greenland coast, and his report spurred Erik.
In Greenland's Western Settlement, earth samples showed that the Vikings used slash-and-burn agriculture. They burned down the birch bushes that originally grew there to create pastures.

Greenland's Norse farms depended on stables called byres to house livestock in winter, and farmers routinely culled their herds, slaughtering animals so the remaining livestock could survive the season. In warmer months the animals went out to pastures, the most fertile of which were controlled by the most powerful farms and the church. In the cooling climate of the Little Ice Age, pasture shrank and winter fodder yields fell, and the culling made it hard to keep livestock, especially for the poorest of the Greenland Norse.

art.text: The Dorset culture produced distinctive triangular end-blades, burins, and oil lamps called qulliq carved from soapstone. These crafted tools and lamps suited the culture's highly cold-adapted hunting lifestyle across the Arctic, which continued into its late phase, dated from 500 to 1000 CE.

The Ipiutak culture, which flourished at Point Hope on Alaska's northwestern coast until it collapsed around 800 CE, is renowned for elaborately carved objects made from ivory, wood, bone, and stone. Its intricate artwork is considered an ancestor of later Inuit art traditions.

The Birnirk culture, which flourished from the 6th to the 12th centuries along Alaska's North Slope and the Chukchi Peninsula, is known for advanced harpoon technology. Their self-pointed harpoon heads featured a single lateral barb and an inset stone side blade, crafted for hunting seals and marine mammals.

The Ipiutak site at Point Hope is renowned for its mortuary offerings, placed in graves with the dead, including openwork ivory carvings and ceremonial masks. One mask represents a human face with facial tattoos, a gaping mouth, and blowfly larvae issuing from its nostrils. Its symbolism is not known for certain: one possibility is a shamanistic meaning connected with Inuit myths about worms, another is an imitation of parasite-infested caribou.

Many Ipiutak houses at Point Hope were built alongside large whale and walrus bones, with whale mandibles used to mark important spaces within the settlement. The site contains more than 500 house depressions, reflecting a hunting society reliant on marine mammals and caribou.

Birnirk hunters on Alaska's North Slope also crafted ice scratchers, tools designed to imitate the sounds of seals moving beneath sea ice. This lure helped attract seals close enough to strike with their harpoons.

A carved maskoid closely resembling the Point Hope mask with facial tattoos was found at Deering, another site linked to the Ipiutak culture, and has been dated to between 600 and 800 CE. Both objects share the same striking style.

Another Ipiutak mask, smaller than the facial-tattoo mask, was found in a coffin with a man, a woman, and a child, placed on the child's chest. It featured cheek and lip plugs along with 14 ivory pendants carved as animals.

Yarn recovered from Willows Island, once suspected to be Norse, was later shown to be Dorset in origin and dates to between 15 BCE and 725 CE. Spun from Arctic hare or muskox fibre at a consistent diameter, it was never woven into fabric.

literature.text: The Greenlanders' oral history was later recorded in the Saga of the Greenlanders and the Saga of Erik the Red. It mentions lands to the south or west that could supply what Greenland lacked, notably Markland, Helluland, and Vinland. Scholars generally believe the voyages have a historical basis, despite some fantastical elements, such as Great Ireland and the uniped who kills Thorvald Eiriksson in Vinland.

The name Vinland appears in the Vinland sagas, which describe a land beyond Greenland, Helluland, and Markland. In Old Norse it was Vínland hit góða, meaning 'Vinland the Good'. The sagas place Leif Erikson's landing there around AD 1000.

The sixth-century historian Procopius wrote of Thule as a large island in the north inhabited by 13 tribes. He says its inhabitants are pagans who practice human sacrifice. Thule was the most northerly place named in ancient Greek and Roman literature, and Procopius wrote of it long after Pytheas first mentioned it.

According to the sagas, Erik the Red was banished from Iceland for three years after killing several men. He sailed west to the lands reported by Gunnbjorn in the late tenth century. Earlier, Snæbjörn Galti's failed settlement on the eastern coast of Greenland had ended with Snæbjörn Galti murdered, the settlement abandoned, and only two colonists surviving the return to Iceland. Erik settled on an island near Tunulliarfik Fjord, and the sagas record that he named the fjord after himself.

The sagas say the Vinland explorers found a land far from Greenland. Archaeologists found remains at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, and Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad discovered them in 1960. Radiocarbon dating confirms the site was occupied for a short period around 1000 CE, matching the sagas' timeframe.

science.text: The Dorset were a Paleo-Eskimo culture whose late phase ran from 500 to 1000 CE. Their history is split into four phases because their hunting and tool-making technologies changed distinctly over time. Typical artifacts include triangular end-blades, soapstone oil lamps called qulliq, and burins.

Unlike a simple spear, the Arctic harpoon had a detachable head designed to toggle, or turn sideways, inside the animal's flesh, which prevented the line from pulling out. Inuit and other Arctic peoples used such specialized harpoons to hunt sea mammals for thousands of years. Some walrus harpoons were sharp, long and pointy, with rawhide wrapped around the wooden shaft, an ivory spear head for easier killing, and an attached ice pick.

The Kayak takes its name from the Inuktitut word qajaq, meaning "man's boat" or "hunter's boat". Each subarctic kayak was built by the man who used it and fitted closely to his size. Builders often used their own body proportions as units of measure.

The Arctic Small Tool tradition links the similar tool use of several Arctic cultures, including the Saqqaq and Pre-Dorset peoples. It was directly ancestral to the Dorset culture, which occupied the North American Arctic from 2700 to 1200 years ago.

The Medieval Warm Period started to warm the Arctic considerably around the mid-10th century. As the climate warmed, the sea ice became less predictable and was isolated from the High Arctic. This change would have strongly affected the Dorset, who depended on hunting on the ice.

Harpoons were built differently to suit different prey. A harpoon impales its target and secures it with barbs or toggling claws, so hunters can use an attached rope to pull the animal in. The Inuit made short, fixed-foreshaft harpoons for hunting at breathing holes. They made loose-shafted harpoons for throwing, which stayed attached to the game after it was struck.

The Thule developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE. The archaeologist Therkel Mathiassen mapped their culture and excavated sites on Baffin Island and around northwestern Hudson Bay. He considered them the remains of a highly developed Eskimo whaling culture that had originated in Alaska.

Kayak paddlers wore a tuilik, a garment stretched over the rim of the kayak coaming and sealed with drawstrings at the coaming, wrists and hood edges. This made the "eskimo roll" the preferred way to recover from capsizing. It mattered because few Inuit could swim and their waters are too cold to survive in for long.

politics.text: According to the history of Greenland, no evidence shows Norsemen knew of the island until the 9th century AD. It was then that Norse Icelandic explorers first settled along its southwestern coast.

Erik the Red was exiled from Iceland around 982 for three years after he killed Eyjolf the Foul and Hrafn the Dueller, and later slew both sons of Thorgest, along with "some other men", in a fight over his father's ornamented pillars. He spent the exile exploring an unknown land to the west, and went on to found the first successful European settlement in Greenland.

Norse settlements in Greenland were established after 986 CE by settlers from Iceland. These colonists became known as the Grænlendingar, the first Europeans to explore and briefly settle North America.

In the 10th century, an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 people lived in Iceland, with a stable social structure and legally secure land ownership. Several years of bad harvests and a famine in the 970s pushed people to look for new places to settle. That search led to the settlement of Greenland after 986 CE.

In the summer of 985, Erik the Red returned to Greenland with a large number of colonists, but of the 25 ships that set out, only 14 arrived. Some of the other 11 turned back, but others were likely lost.

The Icelandic colonists in Greenland founded two settlements on the island's southwest coast: the Eastern Settlement, near present-day Qaqortoq, and the Western Settlement, near present-day Nuuk. Only these areas proved suitable for farming.

In 986, the Icelander Bjarni Herjólfsson became the first European known to sight North America, spotting land after drifting off course on a journey to Greenland. His voyage piqued the interest of later explorers including Leif Eriksson. Leif's brother Thorvald then made the first contact with the native population, later called the skrælings: after attacking and killing eight of the natives, his party was attacked beside their beached ships, and Thorvald was struck under the arm by an arrow, a wound he said would cause his death.

Around the year 1000, Leif Erikson landed in a coastal region of North America the Norse called Vinland, which lay beyond Greenland, Helluland and Markland. This voyage came nearly five centuries before Columbus reached the Americas.

According to the sagas, the Icelanders exiled Erik the Red for three years for committing murder, c. 982. He sailed to Greenland, explored the coastline and claimed certain regions as his own. He then returned to Iceland to persuade people to join him in settling there.
In the Eastern Settlement, Erik the Red built the estate of Brattahlíð, near present-day Narsarsuaq. He held the title of paramount chieftain of Greenland and grew both respected and wealthy.

Norse Greenlanders called the indigenous peoples they encountered in Greenland and Vinland 'Skrælingjar,' a term first recorded in Ari Thorgilsson's work Íslendingabók. The name later gave rise to Kalaallit, used by Greenlandic Inuit for themselves.
The Icelandic sagas say that 25 ships left Iceland with Erik the Red in 985, and only 14 of them arrived safely in Greenland. This shows how risky the crossing to Greenland was.

culture.text: The Dorset were a Paleo-Eskimo culture of the North American Arctic, and their late phase ran from 500 to 1000 CE. Their artifacts include distinctive triangular end-blades, burins, and oil lamps called qulliq that were made of soapstone.
The Thule, or proto-Inuit, were the precursors of all modern Inuit and Yupik peoples. They developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and then expanded eastward across northern Canada.

Norse settlements in Greenland were founded after 986 CE by settlers from Iceland. According to the Saga of the Greenlanders, Erik the Red's son Leif Erikson brought Christianity to Greenland around 1000.

The archaeologist Therkel Mathiassen excavated sites on Baffin Island and around northwestern Hudson Bay. He considered them the remains of a highly developed Eskimo whaling culture that had originated in Alaska and moved to Arctic Canada about 1000 years ago.

Erik the Red was not a Christian according to tradition, but his wife Thjodhild had a small church built some distance from the court. This makes the very early presence of a priest in the colony appear credible.
The Dorset culture is named after Cape Dorset (now Kinngait) in Nunavut, Canada, where western science first found physical evidence of it. It was identified as a separate culture only in 1925.

The Medieval Warm Period began to warm the Arctic considerably around the mid-10th century. The sea ice became less predictable, which would have strongly affected the Dorset, who relied on hunting sea mammals.

The warmer climate of 1000 CE made more of the Arctic habitable and helped populations grow. The search for meteorite iron was probably one impetus for the Alaskan Thule to migrate into northern Canada and Greenland.

Both the Íslendingabók and the Saga of the Greenlanders report that Herjulf Bårdsson, a companion of Erik, had a Christian from the Hebrides on board at the first settlement. Christianity may have arrived with the earliest settlers.

Inuit oral history tells of a people called the Tuniit, whom the Inuit met on arriving in the Arctic. The legends describe them as gentle and shy, speaking a simple language called "Kutak" or "baby-talk", and without bows or arrows, so they were easily killed or driven away. Other versions call the first inhabitants giants, taller and stronger than the Inuit but afraid to interact and "easily put to flight". Some Inuit elders describe peace with this ancient group, while others describe conflict. The Tuniit are linked to the Dorset culture, though how far the legends prove real contact is uncertain.

Although the colony was soon Christianized, there is no archaeological evidence of pagan rituals apart from a few small amulets. The Greenland Norse also appear to have developed their own dialect of Old Norse, now called Greenlandic Norse.
The Thule people, ancestors of modern Inuit, emerged in Alaska around 900 AD. From 1000 onwards they spread eastwards along the Arctic coast, replacing the older Dorset culture.
